title: Redfish Zero to Hero
subtitle: From your first server to a verified rack incident response
intro: Build a mental picture of a server, discover its management interface, and learn to automate from evidence. IPMI comparisons are included throughout.
mode: Hardware-free simulation · no real BMC connection

levels.title: What is a server?
levels.objective: Explain the physical parts before learning any command.

concepts.title: A server answers requests
concepts.explanation:
A server is a computer providing a service to other computers. Your browser is a client when it asks a website for a page. A server receives the request, performs work, and returns a response. The same computer can be a client in one conversation and a server in another.

Hardware is the physical equipment. Software is the set of instructions running on it. Redfish will eventually help us inspect and manage supported hardware; it does not replace the application serving your website.
concepts.analogy: A restaurant customer orders a meal. The kitchen receives the order, does work, and returns it.
concepts.example: A browser requests a product page. A web application on a server reads product data and returns a page. If its power supply fails, the application cannot respond.
concepts.mistake: Server describes a role; it does not mean every server is a giant rack or that a laptop cannot run a server program.

frames.narration: The client wants information.
Its request reaches the server.
The server performs the requested work.
The response goes back to the client; both roles are part of the conversation.

check.prompt: A browser asks a website for a page. What is the browser's role in that conversation?
check.explanation: The browser initiates the request; the website's server handles it.

concepts.title: CPU, memory, and storage
concepts.explanation:
The CPU executes instructions. Memory, usually RAM, holds data that programs are actively using. Storage keeps data such as files when the server is switched off. A network interface connects the server to other machines. These parts cooperate: a file can move from storage into RAM so the CPU can work on it.

More memory can help a workload that is running out of RAM; it does not automatically repair a broken network connection. First identify which component and measurement belong to the problem.
concepts.analogy: The CPU is a worker, RAM is the working desk, and storage is the filing cabinet. A bigger cabinet does not make the desk bigger.
concepts.example: A server has 32 GiB RAM and two processor sockets. Those are different inventory measurements. 32 GiB is a capacity; two is a count of installed processors.
concepts.mistake: RAM and disk capacity both describe sizes, but they are different resources. Processor sockets are also different from CPU cores.

frames.narration: Storage retains the file.
The program loads working data into memory.
The CPU operates on that working data.
A result can be saved back to storage.

check.prompt: Which component holds a running program's temporary working data?
check.explanation: RAM provides working memory. Persistent storage holds saved files.

concepts.title: Power, cooling, and the rack
concepts.explanation:
A rack organizes equipment physically. A power supply converts incoming electrical power into power the server can use. Components release heat as they work; fans and cooling systems remove that heat. Sensors provide observations such as temperature or fan speed. A sensor reading needs a unit and a location to mean something.

Monitoring observes the machine. A technician's maintenance changes the physical machine. An API can report a stalled fan, but a command cannot physically install a replacement fan.
concepts.analogy: A building needs electricity and ventilation as well as rooms. A server needs power and cooling as well as computing parts.
concepts.example: Fan 1 reports 0 RPM while an inlet sensor reports 85 °C. That combination calls for investigation of cooling, using the equipment's own limits and procedures.
concepts.mistake: One high number is not a universal failure rule. A GPU, CPU, inlet, and exhaust sensor can have different operating ranges.

frames.narration: Power enables the equipment to operate.
Work generates heat and cooling carries it away.
A stopped fan can reduce cooling.
The operator collects evidence and plans physical maintenance.

check.prompt: A fan reports 0 RPM. What does RPM describe?
options: Requests per minute in every context
check.explanation: For this fan sensor, RPM is rotational speed; the unit and sensor context matter.

lab.goal: Choose the component that holds working data. The lab retrieves a real response from the simulator and shows its installed capacity.
hints: Think of the working desk and filing cabinet.
RAM is working memory; choose Memory.

questions.prompt: A browser asks a website for a page. What is the browser's role in that conversation?
questions.explanation: The browser initiates the request; the website's server handles it.

questions.prompt: Which component holds a running program's temporary working data?
questions.explanation: RAM provides working memory. Persistent storage holds saved files.

questions.prompt: A fan reports 0 RPM. What does RPM describe?
options: Requests per minute in every context
questions.explanation: For this fan sensor, RPM is rotational speed; the unit and sensor context matter.

questions.prompt: A server has two processor sockets. Does that prove it has two CPU cores?
options: It proves the network is disconnected
No; socket and core counts are different
It proves it has 32 GiB RAM
questions.explanation: A processor can contain multiple cores. Read the relevant inventory field.

questions.prompt: Can a Redfish request physically replace a broken fan?
options: Yes, by changing the temperature unit
Only by deleting the event log
No; physical replacement is a maintenance operation
questions.explanation: An API can expose evidence and supported control actions; a technician handles physical replacement.

levels.title: The management computer inside the server
levels.objective: Separate the host operating system, BMC, management network, and management interface.

concepts.title: Host operating system versus BMC
concepts.explanation:
The host operating system runs the server's applications. A baseboard management controller, or BMC, is an embedded management controller with its own responsibilities. On suitable equipment, it can report hardware information and handle supported management actions independently of the host OS.

That independence is conditional: the BMC still needs power and a reachable management path. A completely unplugged server or disconnected management network may be unreachable. Distinguish an application failure, host failure, and management-controller failure before choosing an action.
concepts.analogy: An apartment's residents use its rooms; the building's control panel separately monitors utilities.
concepts.example: In the host-down lab, the server's PowerState is Off, while its management controller still reports Status.Health = OK.
concepts.mistake: Out-of-band management does not mean management works without any electrical power or network access.

frames.narration: The host and BMC are separate roles.
A host failure can leave the management path working.
The operator asks the BMC for hardware evidence.
Recovery must verify the host as well as the management response.

check.prompt: The host OS is unavailable, but the powered BMC is reachable. Which path can provide hardware evidence?
check.explanation: A reachable BMC can expose management information independently of the host OS.

concepts.title: IPMI and Redfish are interfaces
concepts.explanation:
An interface defines how one program communicates with another. IPMI is an older platform-management interface used by existing equipment and tools. Redfish is a standard for supported management resources and operations using web interface conventions and structured data. They can answer overlapping questions, such as hardware inventory or sensor state.

They are not interchangeable command languages. Vendor implementations and supported operations vary. The IPMI specification is not planned to receive further updates; existing implementations can still be useful. Learn the physical question first, then compare the available interfaces.
concepts.analogy: Two entrances can lead to parts of the same building while using different locks and signs.
concepts.example: The comparison console's educational `ipmitool sensor` mapping shows the same training sensor information as a Redfish read of the Thermal resource. It is a teaching mapping, not native IPMI transport.
concepts.mistake: Do not assume that every IPMI command has an identical Redfish action, especially for shutdown and power-cycle behavior.

frames.narration: Begin with the operational question.
Each interface expresses that question differently.
The resulting observation still needs units and context.
Compare capabilities rather than assuming identical behavior.

check.prompt: What is the best starting point when comparing IPMI and Redfish?
options: The operational question and supported capabilities
Assume IPMI equipment no longer works
check.explanation: Interfaces overlap but differ; installed capabilities and semantics must be checked.

concepts.title: Reachability has several layers
concepts.explanation:
A network address identifies a destination on a network. A management controller may use a dedicated network port or a shared network arrangement, depending on hardware. A request can fail because the destination is wrong, the network is disconnected, the service is unavailable, or access is denied. These are different failures.

A reachable management service is not proof that the host application is healthy. Record which address, service, and operation you tested. Start with observation and distinguish a connection failure from a response saying you lack permission. A ping can succeed while an HTTP login fails: reaching a network destination and authenticating to its service are separate checks.
concepts.analogy: Arriving at a building, finding the right office, and having permission to enter are separate checks.
concepts.example: A connection timeout means no timely response was obtained. An HTTP 403 is a response from a service denying the operation. They require different investigations.
concepts.mistake: Repeatedly rebooting a host will not necessarily fix a management-network cable or authorization problem.

frames.narration: A correct request needs a reachable destination.
Network delivery precedes service processing.
A route failure can prevent delivery entirely.
A delivered request may still be rejected for permissions.

check.prompt: Is an HTTP 403 the same as receiving no network response?
options: It proves the fan is broken
check.explanation: A response and a timeout are different evidence.

lab.goal: Select a management channel that can inspect hardware in both the healthy and host-down scenarios.
hints: The host application depends on the host OS.
Choose BMC and compare host power with management-controller health.

questions.prompt: The host OS is unavailable, but the powered BMC is reachable. Which path can provide hardware evidence?
questions.explanation: A reachable BMC can expose management information independently of the host OS.

questions.prompt: What is the best starting point when comparing IPMI and Redfish?
options: The operational question and supported capabilities
Assume IPMI equipment no longer works
questions.explanation: Interfaces overlap but differ; installed capabilities and semantics must be checked.

questions.prompt: Is an HTTP 403 the same as receiving no network response?
options: It proves the fan is broken
questions.explanation: A response and a timeout are different evidence.

questions.prompt: The BMC works while the host is off. What is still required?
options: BMC power and a reachable management path
questions.explanation: Independent management still depends on power and network arrangements.

questions.prompt: A sensor command succeeds. What has it directly proved?
questions.explanation: A narrow successful observation does not prove all other layers are healthy.

levels.title: Addresses, requests, and JSON
levels.objective: Read a web API response without assuming prior programming knowledge.

concepts.title: An address and a resource path
concepts.explanation:
An HTTPS address identifies a service, and a path identifies a resource within that service. For example, a management service can expose a root resource and links to systems or chassis. A path alone is not a complete remote address. Our simulator only accepts local resource paths, so no training action reaches real equipment.

Use the service's published entry point and follow its links. A URL path is not a physical filesystem path. The server interprets the requested resource and returns a representation of it.
concepts.analogy: The street address gets you to a library; the catalog directs you to a particular subject.
concepts.example: `https://management.example/redfish/v1/` combines a scheme, host, and resource path. `management.example` is an illustrative address. In the app use `/redfish/v1/`.
concepts.mistake: An API path that looks like folders is still a resource identifier; it is not permission to read a computer's files.

frames.narration: An address combines transport, destination, and resource.
Each part answers a different question.
The service interprets the resource path.
Its response represents that resource.

check.prompt: In an API address, what does the resource path select?
check.explanation: The host identifies the service; the path identifies its resource.

concepts.title: Methods and status codes
concepts.explanation:
A request has a method, destination, optional headers, and sometimes a body. GET reads a representation. POST can create something or invoke an advertised action. PATCH requests a partial change. DELETE requests removal of the addressed resource. The exact supported behavior belongs to the resource.

The response contains a status code and may contain data. 200 commonly indicates success, 201 creation, and 202 acceptance of unfinished work. 401 concerns authentication, 403 denied access, 404 absence, and 503 temporary service unavailability. A successful status alone does not prove a physical outcome.
concepts.analogy: Read, create, edit, and remove are different requests you can make of a filing service.
concepts.example: `GET /redfish/v1/` reads the service root. A power action instead uses POST to an advertised action target with a ResetType body.
concepts.mistake: GET is not a generic command to perform any action. Also, 202 means accepted work, not completed work.

frames.narration: GET retrieves information.
An action is validated before execution.
Denied access is a meaningful response.
Accepted asynchronous work must be followed to completion.

check.prompt: What method should retrieve the service root without changing it?
check.explanation: GET is the read operation for a resource representation.

concepts.title: JSON objects, arrays, and values
concepts.explanation:
JSON is a structured text format. An object groups named properties inside braces. An array groups ordered values inside square brackets. Values can be strings, numbers, booleans, null, objects, or arrays. A nested object means you must follow several property names to reach a value. Array positions begin at zero in our pointer reader.

A JSON pointer such as /Status/Health selects a value inside an existing response. It does not make another network request. Read field names and units together, and distinguish a missing property from a property explicitly containing null.
concepts.analogy: An object is a labeled box. An array is an ordered shelf of boxes.
concepts.example: For `{"Status":{"Health":"OK"},"Fans":[{"Reading":6000}]}`, `/Status/Health` selects `OK`; `/Fans/0/Reading` selects `6000`.
concepts.mistake: The number 6000 is not meaningful without its measurement context. Null, missing, and numeric zero are different observations.

frames.narration: Objects associate names with values.
Nested objects require another lookup.
An array requires an index in this exercise.
The pointer selects a value already in the response.

check.prompt: What does /Fans/0/Reading select?
options: Reading on the first Fans array entry
check.explanation: Array index zero refers to the first element.

lab.goal: Read the root resource and select its RedfishVersion string.
hints: Find the resource that owns the information. Follow its advertised links.
A pointer selects a value inside the response; it does not send another request.
Worked plan: GET /redfish/v1/, then select /RedfishVersion.

questions.prompt: In an API address, what does the resource path select?
questions.explanation: The host identifies the service; the path identifies its resource.

questions.prompt: What method should retrieve the service root without changing it?
questions.explanation: GET is the read operation for a resource representation.

questions.prompt: What does /Fans/0/Reading select?
options: Reading on the first Fans array entry
questions.explanation: Array index zero refers to the first element.

questions.prompt: The service replies 202 to a firmware request. What should happen next?
options: Follow the task or monitor link and verify the outcome
questions.explanation: Acceptance and completion are different states.

questions.prompt: A temperature field is absent. Is that the same as 0 °C?
options: No; absent evidence is not a zero measurement
It is always an overheating alert
It proves the server is off
questions.explanation: Missing data can mean unsupported, unavailable, or omitted information.

levels.title: Discover the resource map
levels.objective: Navigate advertised links instead of guessing identifiers.

concepts.title: Start at the service root
concepts.explanation:
The service root is the starting resource for discovering what a Redfish service exposes. It commonly links to collections and services. Read those links instead of constructing an inventory from guessed identifiers. A collection may contain many members or none, and identifiers are implementation-specific.

Our training root advertises Systems, Chassis, Managers, EventService, TaskService, and UpdateService. These are deliberately limited teaching resources. The fixed node names in the simulator are examples, not names to hard-code for real servers.
concepts.analogy: Start at a museum's entrance map; use the exhibits it advertises rather than guessing room numbers.
concepts.example: Read `/redfish/v1/`, select `/Systems/@odata.id`, then issue GET to that returned path.
concepts.mistake: A link is a destination for a new request; selecting a link string from JSON does not fetch the linked resource.

frames.narration: Read the advertised entry point.
Extract the Systems link from the response.
Fetch the linked collection separately.
Then follow its member links.

check.prompt: What is a portable way to find the Systems collection?
options: Always assume a node is named 1
check.explanation: Discovery uses advertised resource links.

concepts.title: Systems, chassis, and managers
concepts.explanation:
A ComputerSystem represents a computing system. A Chassis represents a physical enclosure or related physical assembly. A Manager represents management functionality, such as a BMC. These resources describe different roles, and their relationships can be more complex than one of each per machine.

Choose the resource whose meaning matches your question: processor and memory summary belong to the system; physical cooling often relates to the chassis; controller-specific management information belongs to the manager. Consult links and schemas for the service you actually have.
concepts.analogy: A vehicle, its body, and its control unit describe different aspects of the same equipment.
concepts.example: Our system has MemorySummary, our chassis links to thermal readings, and our manager links to its event log service.
concepts.mistake: Do not assume every chassis contains exactly one system, or every system has exactly one manager.

frames.narration: The resource names describe different roles.
Inventory and observations attach to appropriate resources.
Real relationships can be many-to-many.
Select resources by meaning rather than appearance.

check.prompt: Which resource represents management functionality such as a BMC?
check.explanation: Manager describes management functionality; Chassis and ComputerSystem have different meanings.

concepts.title: Collections and capability discovery
concepts.explanation:
A collection contains links to members. Read its member list, then retrieve the representations you need. Counts summarize the collection; they do not replace the member representations. Supported actions can be advertised in an Actions object, with allowable values or action information describing valid inputs.

Two systems can expose different actions even when they follow the same standard. Some services also paginate collections. The training collection is small and unpaginated; production clients must follow advertised continuation links when present and validate supported values.
concepts.analogy: A directory tells you which offices exist; each office's own sign tells you what services it offers.
concepts.example: node-01 advertises GracefulRestart in its training Reset action. node-02 deliberately advertises a smaller reset-value list. Inspect before invoking.
concepts.mistake: A standard defines resources and semantics; it does not mean every feature is mandatory on every device.

frames.narration: A collection provides member links.
Each member has its own representation.
Their capabilities can differ.
A fleet client handles the differences explicitly.

check.prompt: One server supports an action. What should a fleet client assume about the next server?
options: Its sensor readings must be zero
It supports exactly the same action
check.explanation: Capability discovery is performed per relevant resource.

lab.goal: Extract the advertised Systems collection link from the service root. Return the link string, not the entire root.
hints: Find the resource that owns the information. Follow its advertised links.
A pointer selects a value inside the response; it does not send another request.
Worked plan: GET /redfish/v1/, then select /Systems/@odata.id.

questions.prompt: What is a portable way to find the Systems collection?
options: Always assume a node is named 1
questions.explanation: Discovery uses advertised resource links.

questions.prompt: Which resource represents management functionality such as a BMC?
questions.explanation: Manager describes management functionality; Chassis and ComputerSystem have different meanings.

questions.prompt: One server supports an action. What should a fleet client assume about the next server?
options: Its sensor readings must be zero
It supports exactly the same action
questions.explanation: Capability discovery is performed per relevant resource.

questions.prompt: Does extracting @odata.id automatically fetch that resource?
options: No; a separate request follows the link
questions.explanation: The first operation reads a string from JSON; fetching is another operation.

questions.prompt: A collection has a continuation link. What should an inventory client do?
options: Follow it to collect the remaining members
Assume the first page is complete
questions.explanation: Paged data requires following the advertised continuation mechanism.

levels.title: Inventory with meaningful units
levels.objective: Build an inventory that preserves component meaning, identifiers, and missing information.

concepts.title: Read installed capacity
concepts.explanation:
Inventory answers what equipment exists and what characteristics it reports. It is different from utilization: installed memory capacity does not tell you how much a current application uses. Similarly, an installed processor count is not a CPU utilization percentage. Read each property's definition before comparing values.

Our two training systems have different capacities and processor counts. A useful inventory report retains the system identifier, field, unit, and source. This makes differences visible and avoids adding unlike quantities together.
concepts.analogy: The number of seats in a theater is its capacity; the number occupied at a particular show is utilization.
concepts.example: node-01 reports 32 GiB and two installed processors. node-02 reports 64 GiB and four installed processors. Summing memory gives 96 GiB, not six GiB.
concepts.mistake: Do not label ProcessorSummary.Count as a core count or MemorySummary capacity as currently used RAM.

frames.narration: Each server reports its own inventory.
Keep identifiers while collecting values.
Only sum quantities with compatible meanings and units.
Processor count is a separate inventory column.

check.prompt: What does installed memory capacity tell you?
options: How much memory is reported as installed
Exactly how much a workload currently uses
check.explanation: Capacity and utilization are different measurements.

concepts.title: GB, GiB, count, and reading
concepts.explanation:
A byte is a unit of data size. GB commonly uses decimal powers: one billion bytes. GiB uses binary powers: 1,073,741,824 bytes. A count is a number of items, and a sensor reading observes a particular quantity at a particular time. These values cannot be compared blindly just because they are numeric.

Preserve the reported unit, then convert explicitly if needed. A capacity field that names MiB or GiB should not be relabeled GB without conversion. Also preserve whether a number is a capacity, speed, percentage, temperature, or count.
concepts.analogy: A kilometer and a mile both describe distance, but equal numbers do not describe equal distances.
concepts.example: 32 GiB equals 34,359,738,368 bytes. Two processors is a count. 6000 RPM is a fan speed. They belong in separate columns.
concepts.mistake: Display labels are part of data correctness. Changing a label without converting the value creates a misleading report.

frames.narration: Numbers describe different quantities.
Identify the units before arithmetic.
Convert sizes explicitly using the correct scale.
Keep counts distinct from capacities.

check.prompt: Are 32 GB and 32 GiB exactly equal?
options: No; they use different byte scales
They are equal whenever a vendor uses the same numeral
check.explanation: GB and GiB commonly refer to decimal and binary scales respectively.

concepts.title: Optional and missing inventory
concepts.explanation:
A resource may omit a field because the information is unsupported, unavailable, or not supplied in that representation. A failed read can also prevent collection. A robust report distinguishes a known value, a missing field, and an error collecting the resource. None of those should be silently turned into a zero.

The training inventory is deliberately small. Real inventory can involve more components, pagination, permissions, and changing hardware. Keep enough evidence to explain why a row is incomplete and allow a later retry or human investigation.
concepts.analogy: An unanswered survey question is not the same answer as zero.
concepts.example: Record `capacity: unknown` when a capacity field is absent. Record a collection error if the request returned 503 after bounded retries.
concepts.mistake: Filling all missing values with zero can turn collection failures into false claims that equipment has no memory or no processors.

frames.narration: These are three different kinds of evidence.
Represent each honestly in the report.
Choose an appropriate follow-up.
A complete-looking table is not worth losing uncertainty.

check.prompt: A capacity property is missing. What is an appropriate report value?
check.explanation: Absence does not prove a zero capacity.

lab.goal: Read node-02 and select its installed processor count. Preserve that this is a count, not a utilization percentage.
hints: Find the resource that owns the information. Follow its advertised links.
A pointer selects a value inside the response; it does not send another request.
Worked plan: GET /redfish/v1/Systems/node-02, then select /ProcessorSummary/Count.

questions.prompt: What does installed memory capacity tell you?
options: How much memory is reported as installed
Exactly how much a workload currently uses
questions.explanation: Capacity and utilization are different measurements.

questions.prompt: Are 32 GB and 32 GiB exactly equal?
options: No; they use different byte scales
They are equal whenever a vendor uses the same numeral
questions.explanation: GB and GiB commonly refer to decimal and binary scales respectively.

questions.prompt: A capacity property is missing. What is an appropriate report value?
questions.explanation: Absence does not prove a zero capacity.

questions.prompt: Can processor count and RAM capacity be added into a useful total?
options: Yes; six plus 96 gives a health score
questions.explanation: Meaningful arithmetic requires compatible quantities and units.

questions.prompt: A resource request fails after retries. Which report preserves the evidence?
options: A row showing the collection error and affected resource
questions.explanation: Inventory needs both known values and honest collection failures.

levels.title: Health, temperature, power, and fans
levels.objective: Interpret sensor evidence without confusing state, health, units, or absence.

concepts.title: State and health answer different questions
concepts.explanation:
State describes a resource's operational or lifecycle condition, while health summarizes reported health. A component can be enabled and still unhealthy. Conversely, a deliberately disabled component is not automatically faulty. Read the field definitions and related component information.

In the fan-failure scenario, the fan is Enabled but its Health is Critical and its speed is zero. The chassis also reports degraded health. A summary directs your attention; the individual component and readings explain what to investigate.
concepts.analogy: A shop can be open for business while its refrigerator is broken.
concepts.example: `{"State":"Enabled","Health":"Critical"}` is not contradictory. The fan exists in an enabled state but reports a critical health condition.
concepts.mistake: Do not treat Enabled as a synonym for healthy, or PowerState On as proof that every component works.

frames.narration: A healthy fan has both state and health information.
Its health can change without becoming disabled.
The speed reading provides supporting evidence.
Verify all relevant fields after maintenance.

check.prompt: Can a component be Enabled and have Critical health?
options: It means the sensor unit is missing
Yes; state and health describe different things
check.explanation: Operational state and health are separate properties.

concepts.title: Sensor units and location
concepts.explanation:
A temperature observation needs a location and a unit. A fan observation needs a speed unit or other defined measurement. Power consumption is an instantaneous or interval-defined observation in watts, while energy describes consumption accumulated over time. Read the sensor's own definitions and limits.

The training Thermal resource illustrates a commonly encountered representation. Modern services may advertise ThermalSubsystem, sensors, or other schema resources. Discover those links rather than assuming one older path covers every implementation. Training thresholds are examples, not universal hardware specifications.
concepts.analogy: An outdoor thermometer and an oven thermometer can show very different values without either being wrong.
concepts.example: An inlet reading of 42 °C describes a different location from a processor die sensor. 240 W power is not 240 Wh energy.
concepts.mistake: Comparing readings from different sensor locations or units can create false conclusions about health.

frames.narration: Each measurement has a location and unit.
Preserve those definitions before comparing values.
The failure scenario changes related observations.
Interpret the combination rather than a unitless number.

check.prompt: Is 240 W the same quantity as 240 Wh?
options: No; power and energy are different quantities
check.explanation: Watts measure power; watt-hours measure energy.

concepts.title: Evidence beats one-field diagnosis
concepts.explanation:
A health summary is a useful starting point, but it rarely proves a root cause alone. One sensor is insufficient to diagnose every fault: its value needs equipment, time, and related observations for interpretation. Look for related sensor readings, component health, event messages, and timestamps. Confirm that the observations concern the same equipment and relevant time period. Missing data is a reason to collect more evidence, not automatically a healthy result.

Our incident combines a critical fan, zero speed, high inlet temperature, and an event message. That supports investigating cooling. A real operator would consult hardware documentation, operating conditions, and maintenance procedures before claiming a repair is complete.
concepts.analogy: A smoke alarm tells you to investigate; other observations establish where the problem is.
concepts.example: Read the fan's health and speed, then inspect its related event log. After maintenance, compare the same readings again.
concepts.mistake: Deleting an alarm or event log changes visibility, not the failed physical component.

frames.narration: The summary focuses attention.
Component readings support the diagnosis.
Save evidence before taking action.
Recovery requires re-reading meaningful observations.

check.prompt: Which action proves more about recovery than clearing an alert?
options: Re-read the affected component and related measurements
check.explanation: Verification checks the underlying condition, not just its display.

lab.goal: Read the Thermal resource and select the first fan's Health. Compare the healthy and fan-failure scenarios.
hints: Find the resource that owns the information. Follow its advertised links.
A pointer selects a value inside the response; it does not send another request.
Worked plan: GET /redfish/v1/Chassis/chassis-1/Thermal, then select /Fans/0/Status/Health.

questions.prompt: Can a component be Enabled and have Critical health?
options: It means the sensor unit is missing
Yes; state and health describe different things
questions.explanation: Operational state and health are separate properties.

questions.prompt: Is 240 W the same quantity as 240 Wh?
options: No; power and energy are different quantities
questions.explanation: Watts measure power; watt-hours measure energy.

questions.prompt: Which action proves more about recovery than clearing an alert?
options: Re-read the affected component and related measurements
questions.explanation: Verification checks the underlying condition, not just its display.

questions.prompt: A health property is absent. Can you report OK?
options: Replace the value with the fan speed
questions.explanation: Unknown health is not the same as known healthy status.

questions.prompt: Why compare temperature with fan and event evidence?
options: RPM and Celsius are identical units
Multiple related observations strengthen an investigation
Every high temperature has the same cause
questions.explanation: A diagnosis needs related, correctly interpreted evidence.

levels.title: Logs, events, and IPMI comparisons
levels.objective: Connect observations to timestamped events and understand what each interface actually provides.

concepts.title: An event log records what happened
concepts.explanation:
An event log contains records of noteworthy occurrences. Entries can have an identifier, message, severity, timestamp, and structured message identifier. A record of a past problem is not proof that the problem still exists. Conversely, a current fault might not yet appear in a log you collected earlier.

Use timestamps and identifiers to connect related evidence. The simulator's Training message identifiers are invented for teaching; they are not official message-registry entries. Real Redfish clients may use message registries to interpret standardized message identifiers and arguments.
concepts.analogy: A building's maintenance diary records incidents; a current inspection tells you its condition now.
concepts.example: Our fault scenario records Training.FanStalled at 12:00 UTC. Compare that entry with current fan health and speed rather than assuming every stored critical entry is active.
concepts.mistake: Clearing a log is not physical remediation and can discard evidence needed for investigation.

frames.narration: Initially no failure is observed.
The failure creates an event in our scenario.
The event remains useful historical evidence.
Current health and historical events answer different questions.

check.prompt: A critical log entry remains after maintenance. What should determine current health?
options: A matching message without comparing its timestamp
check.explanation: Historical events and current condition are separate evidence.

concepts.title: Polling and event subscriptions
concepts.explanation:
Polling repeatedly requests current information. An event subscription asks a service to deliver supported notifications when events occur. Polling is easy to reason about but adds request load and can miss short-lived changes between reads. Notifications can reduce repeated reads, but delivery, receiver availability, duplicate messages, and authentication still need attention.

A notification should trigger investigation or an idempotent workflow. It is not a guarantee that every event was delivered exactly once. Our subscription endpoint records a training destination only; it intentionally makes no external callbacks.
concepts.analogy: Polling is checking the mailbox repeatedly. A notification is receiving a doorbell when something arrives.
concepts.example: Create a training subscription using Destination = training://event-inbox. Inspect current state after a notification and periodically reconcile it with reads.
concepts.mistake: Do not assume a notification system removes the need to verify current state or handle duplicates.

frames.narration: Polling samples the current state.
A subscription registers a delivery destination.
An event can trigger a notification.
The receiver verifies state and handles duplicates.

check.prompt: What is a sensible response to a hardware event notification?
options: Inspect relevant current state and handle possible duplicates
check.explanation: Event delivery and current-state verification are complementary.

concepts.title: Sensors, inventory, and logs across IPMI
concepts.explanation:
IPMI tooling commonly exposes sensor information, sensor data records, inventory information, and a system event log. These support operational questions that overlap with Redfish resources. A sensor data record helps describe a sensor; an event record describes an occurrence. Neither should be confused with the physical component itself.

Our console accepts a small educational command vocabulary: sensor, sdr, fru print, sel list, and chassis power status. It reads the same training objects through simplified mappings. Native IPMI transport, binary records, vendor extensions, and complete ipmitool behavior are beyond this simulator.
concepts.analogy: The same maintenance investigation can use two differently organized reference books.
concepts.example: Compare `ipmitool sel list` with the Redfish EventLog Entries response; compare `ipmitool sensor` with the training Thermal response.
concepts.mistake: Our mapping teaches overlapping questions. It does not establish full semantic equivalence or validate native IPMI interoperability.

frames.narration: Compare event information.
Compare sensor information and definitions.
Compare inventory questions.
Compare a supported state read while preserving interface differences.

check.prompt: What kind of information does sel list describe in this teaching console?
check.explanation: SEL is the system-event-log vocabulary used by IPMI tooling.

lab.goal: Read the event log and select the first entry's MessageId. Compare healthy and fan-failure messages.
hints: Find the resource that owns the information. Follow its advertised links.
A pointer selects a value inside the response; it does not send another request.
Worked plan: GET /redfish/v1/Managers/bmc-1/LogServices/EventLog/Entries, then select /Members/0/MessageId.

options: A matching message without comparing its timestamp
questions.explanation: Historical events and current condition are separate evidence.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible response to a hardware event notification?
options: Inspect relevant current state and handle possible duplicates
questions.explanation: Event delivery and current-state verification are complementary.

questions.prompt: What kind of information does sel list describe in this teaching console?
questions.explanation: SEL is the system-event-log vocabulary used by IPMI tooling.

questions.prompt: A duplicate event is received. What property should the response workflow have?
options: It should repeat every action blindly
It should avoid repeating unnecessary side effects
questions.explanation: Deduplication and idempotent response handling prevent duplicate effects.

questions.prompt: Does this app's IPMI console test native IPMI transport?
options: No; it is an explicitly labeled teaching mapping
Yes, it uses your real BMC
questions.explanation: The simulator does not access a real BMC or implement native IPMI transport.

levels.title: Power and boot actions
levels.objective: Preview, authorize, execute, and verify supported actions in a simulation.

concepts.title: Power is an action with consequences
concepts.explanation:
Reading PowerState observes a condition. Requesting a power or reset action changes a system. A service advertises the action target and supported ResetType values. Choose a supported value whose meaning matches the task. Graceful shutdown or restart requests coordinated behavior; forceful operations can have different consequences and support.

The simulator only implements its advertised subset. A real operator considers workload state, maintenance procedures, permissions, and the server's actual capabilities. After a request, re-read relevant state. A response that accepts an action is not universal proof that applications recovered.
concepts.analogy: Looking at a light switch differs from operating it; changing the switch affects everyone using the room.
concepts.example: In this lab, POST the node-01 Reset action with ResetType = GracefulRestart, then verify the simulated restart count and resulting PowerState.
concepts.mistake: IPMI power-cycle and a graceful Redfish restart must not be assumed identical. The comparison console labels its simplified mapping.

frames.narration: Discover the supported action.
Choose the appropriate advertised value.
Perform the authorized simulated action.
Verify the hardware state and remember the application layer.

check.prompt: Before a reset, where should you look for valid ResetType values?
options: A random vendor blog for another model
check.explanation: Supported values belong to the actual resource and service.

concepts.title: Permissions and an action preview
concepts.explanation:
Authentication establishes an identity. Authorization decides what that identity may do. A reader can inspect information while an operator may be allowed to change state. A useful action preview identifies the target, requested change, expected consequence, and verification step before execution.

Our simulator has viewer and operator roles plus explicit confirmation for modifications. This is a teaching boundary, not a complete production authorization system. Real deployments require their own identity provider, access controls, audit policy, and carefully scoped hardware permissions.
concepts.analogy: A visitor badge and a maintenance key identify different permitted activities.
concepts.example: Try a reset as viewer: it returns 403. Change to operator, review the plan, and confirm the simulated action. An unconfirmed operation returns 409 in our teaching API.
concepts.mistake: Logging in successfully does not imply permission to perform every operation.

frames.narration: The role establishes allowed operations.
A reader's modification is rejected.
An operator still reviews the action.
Execution is followed by evidence and an audit record.

check.prompt: A viewer logs in successfully. Can it necessarily reset the server?
options: Yes, every login is administrator access
A token automatically grants the action when its request is valid JSON
A known system ID automatically authorizes any action
check.explanation: Identity and permission are separate checks.

concepts.title: Boot overrides and one-time intent
concepts.explanation:
A boot override can request a supported source for a future boot. It does not mean that source is reachable or that a boot succeeded. Services expose their own supported targets and enablement behavior. A one-time override should not be confused with a permanently changed boot order.

The simulator advertises a small Boot subset and models a one-time target during a restart. It does not perform network boot or install an operating system. On real equipment, verify supported fields, provisioning dependencies, and the subsequent system and application outcome.
concepts.analogy: Choosing a different train for one trip does not rewrite your daily commute permanently.
concepts.example: In the console, PATCH node-01 Boot with BootSourceOverrideTarget = Pxe and BootSourceOverrideEnabled = Once. Restart and inspect the training LastBootTarget and cleared override.
concepts.mistake: Selecting PXE is not proof that DHCP, network boot services, images, and installation are correctly configured.

frames.narration: A running system has not booted again yet.
The override expresses intent for a future boot.
The teaching restart consumes one-time intent.
Real boot success needs separate verification.

check.prompt: What does a one-time boot override describe?
options: Intent for a supported future boot
check.explanation: A requested boot source and successful provisioning are different outcomes.

lab.goal: Perform exactly one simulated graceful restart on node-01. Use the operator role, review the consequence, and confirm the change.
hints: Read the action's allowed values in the console.
On is not a restart. Use GracefulRestart with the operator role and confirmation.

options: A random vendor blog for another model
questions.explanation: Supported values belong to the actual resource and service.

options: Yes, every login is administrator access
A token automatically grants the action when its request is valid JSON
A known system ID automatically authorizes any action
questions.explanation: Identity and permission are separate checks.

questions.prompt: What does a one-time boot override describe?
options: Intent for a supported future boot
questions.explanation: A requested boot source and successful provisioning are different outcomes.

questions.prompt: A restart request succeeds. What still needs verification?
options: The intended hardware and workload outcome
questions.explanation: A successful request and a recovered workload are separate evidence.

questions.prompt: Are native IPMI power-cycle and graceful Redfish restart universally interchangeable?
options: No; inspect the operations' actual semantics
questions.explanation: Power and reset operations differ in coordination, support, and consequences.

levels.title: BIOS, firmware, and asynchronous work
levels.objective: Distinguish pending intent, running work, and verified completion.

concepts.title: Active versus pending BIOS settings
concepts.explanation:
A BIOS setting controls part of the system's startup configuration. A service may expose active settings and a separate settings object where changes are staged. The pending representation expresses requested configuration. It does not prove the running or next-boot configuration has changed.

Use the advertised settings link and supported values. Some changes require a reset, and dependencies vary by equipment. The training model stages BootMode and applies it during a graceful restart. Verify the active representation after the modeled application point.
concepts.analogy: Editing tomorrow's schedule does not mean today's meeting has already moved.
concepts.example: PATCH the advertised Bios/Settings object to request BootMode = Uefi. The active Bios remains Legacy until the training restart applies the pending setting.
concepts.mistake: Do not report a pending value as active just because PATCH returned success.

frames.narration: Read the current active setting.
Stage a requested change separately.
The modeled application point applies the pending intent.
Verify the active value after it happens.

check.prompt: PATCH stages a BIOS value. Where should you verify it after application?
check.explanation: Pending intent and active state must be distinguished.

concepts.title: Tasks describe unfinished work
concepts.explanation:
Some operations take longer than one request. A service can accept the request and expose a task or task monitor. Poll the advertised monitor according to its semantics, observe progress and terminal status, and handle both successful and unsuccessful completion. A percentage alone is not enough to classify the result.

The simulator advances a firmware task as it is read. That is a deliberate teaching simplification, not a production scheduling mechanism. Real operations can fail, time out, require resets, or have vendor-specific conditions. Verification must include the managed resource afterward.
concepts.analogy: A repair ticket marked accepted is different from one marked completed and inspected.
concepts.example: The training update returns 202 and a Location link. Follow the task from Running to Completed, then read FirmwareInventory/bmc to verify demo-2.0.
concepts.mistake: Do not busy-poll indefinitely or interpret 100 percent as success without checking the terminal state and result.

frames.narration: Submitting starts the workflow.
Acceptance creates work to follow.
Progress is intermediate evidence.
Completion and resource verification finish the workflow.

check.prompt: Does HTTP 202 mean firmware installation is finished?
options: It means the request was unauthenticated
It means the BMC has no power
No; follow the task and verify the version
check.explanation: 202 describes acceptance, not completion.

concepts.title: Firmware management is a lifecycle
concepts.explanation:
Firmware is software embedded in equipment or its controllers. Updating it involves identifying the component, checking a compatible image and supported update method, scheduling the operation, following progress, and verifying the resulting version and health. Inventory is part of the decision, not just a report afterward.

Our simulator accepts only a built-in training firmware URI and performs no downloads. It cannot test compatibility, signatures, rollback, or physical flash behavior. The same lifecycle concepts prepare you to read vendor procedures and evaluate a real maintenance plan.
concepts.analogy: Replacing a building's control software requires the right version, a scheduled change, and checks afterward.
concepts.example: POST the advertised SimpleUpdate target with ImageURI = training://firmware/demo-2.0. Follow the returned task and read the firmware inventory again.
concepts.mistake: A newer-looking version string alone is not a compatibility or safety assessment.

frames.narration: Identify the component and its current version.
Plan the intended update and verification.
Follow the running work.
Inspect the result rather than trusting the initial request.

check.prompt: What does the simulated update validate about a real firmware image?
options: Nothing about physical compatibility or flashing
check.explanation: The built-in teaching image is a simulation, not hardware qualification.

lab.goal: Stage BootMode = Uefi, then apply it with a simulated graceful restart. Verify that active settings changed while the before-reset snapshot remained Legacy.

fields.name: confirmed
fields.label: I reviewed the pending change and restart

hints: A pending setting alone does not change active state.
Use Uefi, operator permission, and a confirmed GracefulRestart.

questions.prompt: PATCH stages a BIOS value. Where should you verify it after application?
questions.explanation: Pending intent and active state must be distinguished.

questions.prompt: Does HTTP 202 mean firmware installation is finished?
options: It means the request was unauthenticated
It means the BMC has no power
No; follow the task and verify the version
questions.explanation: 202 describes acceptance, not completion.

questions.prompt: What does the simulated update validate about a real firmware image?
options: Nothing about physical compatibility or flashing
questions.explanation: The built-in teaching image is a simulation, not hardware qualification.

questions.prompt: A task reaches a failed terminal state. What is the correct interpretation?
options: The operation failed; inspect task details and resource state
It succeeded because it was accepted earlier
questions.explanation: Terminal state and managed-resource evidence determine the outcome.

questions.prompt: Where should a client find the supported settings object?
questions.explanation: Use discovery for settings as well as inventory and actions.

levels.title: Python fleet automation
levels.objective: Discover a fleet, bound failures and concurrency, and retain useful results.

concepts.title: Turn discovery into a Python loop
concepts.explanation:
Automation repeats a well-defined operation over discovered resources. Start at the root, retrieve the systems collection, follow each member link, and collect fields into a report. Separate successful rows from failed reads so one bad resource does not fabricate data or silently erase equipment from the inventory.

The example CLI includes a real HTTP client for the local simulator. It uses a request timeout, session token, bounded retries for selected transient reads, and a report containing per-resource outcomes. It intentionally performs no hardware-changing actions.
concepts.analogy: Use a directory to visit each listed office and record both answers and unavailable offices.
concepts.example: Python: `root = client.get('/redfish/v1/'); members = client.get(root['Systems']['@odata.id'])['Members']`. Then read each member's @odata.id.
concepts.mistake: Automating a guessed node-01 path is not fleet discovery, and catching every error as an empty success loses evidence.

frames.narration: Discovery defines the actual workload.
Member links identify the resources.
Every read has an outcome to retain.
A useful report preserves incomplete evidence.

check.prompt: How should an inventory automation find systems?
options: Discover the collection and follow member links
Use a sensor value as a URL
check.explanation: Discovery makes the loop portable across supported resource identifiers.

concepts.title: Bound retries and concurrency
concepts.explanation:
A timeout bounds how long a request can wait. A retry is another attempt after a chosen failure. Concurrency allows a limited number of operations to be in progress together. Each needs an explicit bound so a fleet script cannot overwhelm services or run forever. Retry behavior should depend on the operation and response.

Our inventory retries selected transient GET failures and limits workers. Production clients also need backoff, jitter, rate-limit handling, cancellation, and operational budgets. Do not blindly retry a destructive action: it may already have succeeded despite a lost response.
concepts.analogy: A queue with a few service desks is manageable; unlimited crowds and endless retries are not.
concepts.example: The transfer scenario injects one 503 for node-02. At least one bounded retry lets the read recover; zero retries leaves an explicit failed row.
concepts.mistake: A safe retry policy for a GET is not automatically a safe retry policy for a POST action.

frames.narration: A read can encounter a transient failure.
The selected policy permits another attempt.
A bounded retry recovers this scenario.
Action retries need separate reasoning and semantics.

check.prompt: A POST response is lost. Should the client blindly repeat the action forever?
options: No; determine the operation's result and safe retry semantics
check.explanation: A lost response does not prove that the server did not perform the action.

concepts.title: Sessions, least privilege, and audit
concepts.explanation:
A session token represents an authenticated session and should be treated as a secret. Send it through the expected header over protected transport, restrict its lifetime, and remove it from logs. Least privilege means granting only the operations needed by the task. Inventory automation can normally use a reader role.

Audit records help explain which identity requested which operation on which resource. Our simulator deliberately excludes token and password values from its audit. A production deployment needs its own authentication and retention policy; a shared teaching instance is not a management gateway.
concepts.analogy: Borrow the key for the room you need, return it afterward, and record the maintenance visit without publishing the key.
concepts.example: The demo session response returns X-Auth-Token in a header. The CLI keeps it in memory, uses viewer for inventory, and deletes its session when finished.
concepts.mistake: A token should not be pasted into a public issue, included in a URL, or recorded in a tutorial screenshot.

frames.narration: Authentication creates a scoped session.
The reader performs only needed operations.
The report preserves results, not credentials.
Cleanup ends the session's use.

check.prompt: Which role fits a read-only inventory task in this simulator?
check.explanation: Use the least privilege needed for the operation.

lab.goal: Collect both systems with bounded workers and retries. Your plan must succeed when node-02 returns one transient 503.
hints: Inspect whether a failed row is being preserved.
Allow at least one bounded retry for the injected 503; keep worker count bounded.

questions.prompt: How should an inventory automation find systems?
options: Discover the collection and follow member links
Use a sensor value as a URL
questions.explanation: Discovery makes the loop portable across supported resource identifiers.

questions.prompt: A POST response is lost. Should the client blindly repeat the action forever?
options: No; determine the operation's result and safe retry semantics
questions.explanation: A lost response does not prove that the server did not perform the action.

questions.prompt: Which role fits a read-only inventory task in this simulator?
questions.explanation: Use the least privilege needed for the operation.

questions.prompt: Where should a session token appear in an inventory report?
questions.explanation: Reports need operational evidence rather than reusable credentials.

questions.prompt: A fleet has mixed capabilities. Which automation is more reliable?
options: Discover and handle capabilities per resource
Send every action to every server
questions.explanation: Fleet automation must handle differences and missing features explicitly.

levels.title: A rack incident from evidence to recovery
levels.objective: Diagnose the affected layer, choose an appropriate response, and prove the simulated recovery.

concepts.title: Connect hardware, metrics, and logs
concepts.explanation:
Hardware management, numerical telemetry, and event logs offer complementary evidence. Redfish can identify the physical component and its current reported condition. Metrics can show how readings change over time. Logs can provide timestamped events and application symptoms. Correlate them using consistent equipment identifiers and relevant time windows.

Our scenario exposes training Prometheus-format fan and temperature metrics beside Redfish data. SPL and PromQL examples illustrate investigations, but this simulator does not run Splunk or a full PromQL engine. Your existing courses provide those query skills.
concepts.analogy: A map tells you where, a thermometer tells you how much, and a diary tells you what happened.
concepts.example: PromQL idea: `training_fan_speed_rpm == 0`. Redfish provides the fan MemberId and Health; an event log provides the associated message and time.
concepts.mistake: A shared timestamp alone does not establish a shared cause. Match component identifiers and consider other explanations.

frames.narration: Each source provides different evidence.
Match the stalled fan across representations.
Inspect related conditions and symptoms.
Build a diagnosis from consistent observations.

check.prompt: What should connect hardware, metrics, and log evidence?
options: Consistent equipment identifiers and relevant time windows
Only matching health text, without device identity
check.explanation: Correlation depends on the same equipment and relevant timing.

concepts.title: Choose a response for the failed layer
concepts.explanation:
A hardware cooling failure is not repaired by hiding telemetry. A host restart might change symptoms without repairing a physical fan. First identify the failed layer, collect supporting evidence, and select a response appropriate to that layer. Physical maintenance requires a technician and the equipment's procedures.

The training maintenance endpoint models fan replacement so you can inspect before/after values without hardware. It is our simulation extension, not a standard Redfish API. The plan should leave a healthy system unchanged and act only when the relevant failure evidence is present.
concepts.analogy: Turning a building's lights off does not fix its broken ventilation fan.
concepts.example: The capstone policy detects a critical fan with zero RPM, models technician replacement, and re-reads thermal information. It performs no maintenance in the healthy case.
concepts.mistake: Always-restart policies can add disruption while leaving the original fault untouched.

frames.narration: Healthy evidence calls for no maintenance.
Failure evidence directs the investigation.
The response addresses the physical fault in the teaching model.
The plan avoids unrelated disruptions.

check.prompt: Which response best matches a confirmed physical fan failure?
options: Appropriate cooling maintenance followed by verification
check.explanation: The response should address the failed layer.

concepts.title: A hero verifies and explains limits
concepts.explanation:
A useful incident report records the symptom, affected equipment, evidence, hypothesis, response, verification, and remaining uncertainty. Verification reads meaningful state after the response and checks whether the expected condition changed. To verify a repair, re-read the affected subsystem and check the original symptom; that does not prove every other subsystem is healthy. It should also check for unintended consequences and continuing application impact.

Passing this course demonstrates the training objectives in bounded scenarios. It does not certify vendor interoperability or qualify every production action. Transfer your reasoning to real equipment through supervised reads, vendor documentation, and maintenance practice before independently managing a fleet.
concepts.analogy: A repair is credible when the mechanic shows the before and after inspection, not just the receipt.
concepts.example: In the training recovery, fan speed returns to 6000 RPM, fan Health becomes OK, and the modeled inlet temperature returns to 42 °C. Real cooling changes may take time and need further checks.
concepts.mistake: One passing lab is not proof that all real equipment, failures, and workloads behave the same way.

frames.narration: Save the initial evidence.
Record the response and collect new observations.
Verify the relevant conditions and other layers.
Explain what the training result establishes and what remains untested.

check.prompt: What should a credible recovery report contain?
options: A success response without re-reading the affected state
A claim that every vendor is certified
check.explanation: Verification and honest scope are part of operational competence.

lab.goal: Implement a conditional response: leave healthy equipment alone, identify a stalled critical fan, model its replacement, and verify recovered fan and temperature readings.
hints: The healthy scenario should require no maintenance.
Choose replace_failed_fan with operator permission and confirmation. Inspect all before/after evidence.

questions.prompt: What should connect hardware, metrics, and log evidence?
options: Consistent equipment identifiers and relevant time windows
Only matching health text, without device identity
questions.explanation: Correlation depends on the same equipment and relevant timing.

questions.prompt: Which response best matches a confirmed physical fan failure?
options: Appropriate cooling maintenance followed by verification
questions.explanation: The response should address the failed layer.

questions.prompt: What should a credible recovery report contain?
options: A success response without re-reading the affected state
A claim that every vendor is certified
questions.explanation: Verification and honest scope are part of operational competence.

questions.prompt: Why must the capstone also test a healthy scenario?
options: To verify that the policy avoids unnecessary changes
questions.explanation: A conditional response must handle both failure and no-failure cases.

questions.prompt: What is the next step after completing the simulation course?
options: Validate the reasoning with supervised real hardware and vendor procedures
Assume all production systems are identical
questions.explanation: Simulation teaches reasoning while hardware-specific operational competence still needs real validation.

glossary.server: A computer or program providing a service to clients.
glossary.client: A program initiating a request to a service.
glossary.hardware: Physical equipment such as processors, memory, fans, and power supplies.
glossary.CPU: Processor that executes instructions; socket and core counts are different.
glossary.RAM: Memory holding actively used working data.
glossary.GB: One billion bytes, a decimal size unit.
glossary.power supply: Equipment converting input power for server components.
glossary.sensor: A source of a defined measurement such as temperature.
glossary.RPM: Rotations per minute for a rotational-speed reading.
glossary.host: The main computing system running the host operating system.
glossary.operating system: Software managing a computer's resources and programs.
glossary.BMC: Baseboard management controller, an embedded management controller.
glossary.out-of-band: Management independent of the host OS, still dependent on power and connectivity.
glossary.interface: An agreed way for systems or programs to communicate.
glossary.IPMI: Intelligent Platform Management Interface, used by existing equipment and tools.
glossary.Redfish: DMTF's structured management standard using RESTful interface semantics.
glossary.IP address: A network-layer address for a destination.
glossary.timeout: A limit on waiting for a response.
glossary.permission: Authorization to perform a particular operation.
glossary.URL: Address describing transport, host, and resource path.
glossary.HTTPS: HTTP protected by TLS transport security.
glossary.resource: An addressable management entity represented by API data.
glossary.GET: Request to read a resource representation.
glossary.POST: Request commonly used to create a resource or invoke an advertised action.
glossary.PATCH: Request for a supported partial resource change.
glossary.HTTP status: Code reporting how a service handled a request.
glossary.JSON: Structured text containing objects, arrays, and typed values.
glossary.object: JSON association of property names with values.
glossary.JSON pointer: Path selecting a value inside JSON; it does not fetch another resource.
glossary.null: Explicit JSON value indicating no value, distinct from missing or zero.
glossary.service root: The discovery entry point for a Redfish service.
glossary.ComputerSystem: Redfish resource describing a computing system.
glossary.Chassis: Redfish resource describing a physical assembly or enclosure.
glossary.capability: An operation or property actually supported by a resource.
glossary.pagination: Splitting a collection across representations linked by continuation.
glossary.capacity: The reported total available size or amount.
glossary.utilization: Observed use of a resource over a defined interval.
glossary.State: A resource's operational or lifecycle condition.
glossary.Health: A reported health assessment, separate from state.
glossary.watts: Unit of power, distinct from energy.
glossary.energy: Consumption accumulated over time, such as watt-hours or joules.
glossary.evidence: Observations supporting or challenging a conclusion.
glossary.diagnosis: An explanation evaluated against relevant evidence.
glossary.event: A noteworthy occurrence represented as a record or notification.
glossary.timestamp: Time associated with an observation or event.
glossary.message registry: Definitions explaining standardized message identifiers and arguments.
glossary.idempotent: Repeating an operation has no additional intended effect beyond one successful application.
glossary.SDR: Sensor data record in IPMI vocabulary.
glossary.SEL: System event log in IPMI vocabulary.
glossary.action: An advertised operation that may change state.
glossary.ResetType: A supported input describing a requested reset or power action.
glossary.authorization: Deciding which operations an identity may perform.
glossary.audit: Record of relevant operations and actors, excluding reusable secrets.
glossary.boot override: Supported intent changing a future boot's source or behavior.
glossary.PXE: A network-boot mechanism requiring its own provisioning dependencies.
glossary.BIOS: System firmware and startup configuration; commonly used as an API resource name.
glossary.UEFI: Modern firmware interface and boot environment; supported modes vary.
glossary.task: Representation or monitor for asynchronous work.
glossary.firmware: Software embedded in equipment or controllers.
glossary.automation: Repeating a defined workflow using software.
glossary.retry: Another bounded attempt after a selected failure.
glossary.concurrency: A bounded number of operations in progress together.
glossary.least privilege: Only the permissions required for the task.
glossary.maintenance: Planned intervention appropriate to equipment and workload needs.
glossary.metrics: Numerical observations with labels, units, and timing.
glossary.verification: Checking evidence of the intended outcome after an operation.
